content: Martha was diagnosed with bipolar affective disorder and was prescribed lithium to help stabilize her mood. Thirteen days later, her father found her lifeless on the floor of her bedroom. She had suffered a fatal cardiac arrhythmia at the age of twenty-two. Tragically, she was unable to reach the door to call for help. Despite the series of medical errors and an adverse reaction to the medication that led to her death, no formal reporting occurred, and her death was classified as natural. It took six years of relentless effort, significant media attention, and two additional death reviews to finalize the investigation into Martha’s death and implement meaningful changes aimed at preventing similar tragedies. Two key lessons emerge from this case: first, individuals can encourage and even personally report adverse medication events; second, patients and their families can take an active role in managing medical care and medication safety. Honoring individuals like Martha requires transparency and centralized reporting of such events, ensuring that these tragedies lead to improved medication safety for all. Medication errors are particularly impactful in high-risk clinical situations, such as inpatient hospital settings, where acute or complex conditions often necessitate intricate medication regimens. Vulnerable populations, including young children, the elderly, and those with kidney or liver disease, are at heightened risk of adverse outcomes. Common errors in these scenarios include incorrect dosing, improper administration routes, and failure to adhere to treatment protocols. Identifying high-risk situations and medications is critical to reducing harm. Polypharmacy, defined as the concurrent use of four or more medications, has become increasingly common due to longer life expectancies and the prevalence of chronic diseases in older populations. While necessary in many cases, polypharmacy increases the risk of side effects, drug interactions, and challenges with adherence. To mitigate these risks, medications must be prescribed and managed optimally, ensuring measurable benefits with minimal adverse effects. Standardized policies, procedures, and protocols are essential, from initial prescribing to regular medication reviews. Patients, when equipped with the right information and tools, can play a vital role in making informed decisions about their medications. Technology can also assist in this process. Transitions of care, such as hospital admissions or discharges, are particularly vulnerable to communication errors, which can result in serious medication mistakes. Effective communication, including formal medication reconciliation processes, is crucial during these transitions. Patients can actively contribute by maintaining an up-to-date list of their medications, ensuring accuracy during care transitions. The World Health Organization (WHO) has launched the third Global Patient Safety Challenge, focusing on medication safety. This initiative calls on member states to prioritize medication safety at the national level, aiming to significantly reduce avoidable harm related to medications within five years. The framework emphasizes early action in high-risk situations, polypharmacy, and care transitions. It also advocates for national coordination, patient education, and regular progress assessments. WHO will support this initiative by leading global efforts, facilitating country-specific programs, commissioning expert reports, developing safety strategies and tools, and promoting research on medication-related harm. Regional events, advocacy campaigns, and patient involvement will further drive the initiative. Monitoring and evaluation will ensure progress, while resources will be mobilized to enable full implementation. Collaboration with a wide range of stakeholders, including ministries of health, healthcare leaders, educational institutions, regulatory agencies, patient advocacy groups, and the pharmaceutical industry, is essential to achieving the goals of this challenge. By working together, these entities can create safer medication practices and reduce harm on a global scale.
